title: Environment & VPD
purpose: Expand Environment & VPD from a five-section overview into a measurement-first environmental systems curriculum while preserving the existing V3 topic owner and V4 guided-study layer.
learningOutcome: A learner should be able to describe what the plant actually experiences rather than relying on a room-average setpoint; distinguish air temperature from leaf temperature; explain RH, vapor pressure, dew point, air VPD and leaf VPD; connect atmospheric demand to stomata, transpiration and root-zone supply; distinguish circulation from ventilation and moisture removal; understand CO2 as both a plant input and a life-safety concern; qualify sensor placement and calibration; map canopy microclimates; and use trends, transitions and risk-reviewed control envelopes instead of universal target charts.
visualTargets: air temperature versus leaf temperature and energy balance
infrared leaf-temperature measurement geometry and field of view
relative humidity, saturation vapor pressure and dew point relationship
condensation risk when a surface falls below dew point
air VPD versus leaf VPD comparison
VPD calculation and interpretation without universal target claims
stomata, transpiration and the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum
boundary layer thinning with air movement
canopy microclimate mapping and dead zones
CO2 supply, canopy distribution, ventilation loss and safety separation
sensor placement, shielding, calibration and mapping
stage-aware control bands, warnings, alarms and transition records

chapters.title: Measurement, Sensors & Canopy Mapping
chapters.objective: Build a defensible environmental measurement system before interpreting climate numbers or changing equipment.

lessons.title: A sensor measures its location, not the whole room
lessons.summary: Treat every temperature, RH, CO2 or substrate reading as a measurement taken at a defined location and exposure rather than as a universal description of the crop environment.
lessons.cultivation: A stable wall or controller reading can coexist with hot tops, humid flower pockets, cold corners or weakly mixed lower canopy zones.
lessons.observe: Record sensor height, orientation, shielding, nearby equipment, plant distance and operating state before interpreting the number.

lessons.title: Control sensors, mapping sensors and safety sensors serve different jobs
lessons.summary: Separate the instrument that drives equipment from temporary or fixed instruments used to map spatial conditions and from independent devices used for life-safety monitoring.
lessons.cultivation: One sensor architecture should not silently stand in for every purpose, especially where CO2 safety or localized canopy risk is involved.
lessons.observe: Maintain a sensor register with unique IDs, role, model, serial number, range, accuracy, location and data-system channel.

lessons.title: Calibration, verification and disagreement
lessons.summary: Use traceable comparisons, stated tolerances and as-found/as-left records to distinguish real environmental differences from sensor drift or measurement bias.
lessons.cultivation: A climate decision based on a biased RH or temperature sensor can push equipment in the wrong direction while still producing a neat data trace.
lessons.observe: When instruments disagree, investigate placement, stabilization, contamination, clock sync and calibration before averaging the readings.

lessons.title: Map occupied-canopy microclimates across operating states
lessons.summary: Survey the crop at multiple heights and positions during representative lights-on, peak-load, irrigation, lights-off and equipment-cycle states.
lessons.cultivation: Plants change airflow, heat, water-vapor release and CO2 distribution, so an empty-room map cannot permanently qualify a full canopy.
lessons.observe: Compare minimum, median, maximum and duration outside the intended envelope rather than relying only on room averages.

knowledgeChecks: Why can a controller reading be accurate but still unrepresentative of the canopy?
What is the difference between a control sensor and a diagnostic mapping sensor?
Why should two disagreeing sensors not simply be averaged?
Which operating states should be included when qualifying an occupied-canopy map?

chapters.title: Air Temperature, Leaf Temperature & Energy Balance
chapters.objective: Understand why tissue temperature can differ from room air and how radiation, transpiration, convection, water supply and equipment state create that difference.

lessons.title: Air temperature is context, leaf temperature is tissue condition
lessons.summary: Separate the temperature of surrounding air from the temperature of the photosynthetic surface whose energy balance is altered by radiation, evaporation and convection.
lessons.cultivation: Leaf temperature can rise above air under radiant load or fall below it when transpiration and convection remove enough heat.
lessons.observe: Pair canopy air temperature with repeatable leaf-temperature measurements instead of assuming the two values are identical.

lessons.title: Measure leaf temperature without measuring the background
lessons.summary: Use infrared instruments with attention to emissivity, distance-to-spot ratio, field of view, target fill, reflections and sampling geometry.
lessons.cultivation: An IR gun can report a precise-looking mixed temperature if the measurement spot includes wall, pot, fixture or several leaves.
lessons.observe: Document leaf class, canopy zone, angle, distance, lit or shaded state and instrument settings for repeatable comparisons.

lessons.title: Heat load is duration, tissue state and location—not one room number
lessons.summary: Distinguish warm growth conditions from damaging heat stress by considering tissue temperature, duration, water supply, root-zone temperature, developmental stage and plant response.
lessons.cultivation: Fixture heat, sunlit surfaces, failed cooling, warm roots or weak transpiration can create local stress that disappears in the average room temperature.
lessons.observe: Map air, leaf and root-zone temperature together with PPFD, irrigation status and HVAC state before assigning cause.

lessons.title: Cold exposure can suppress function above freezing
lessons.summary: Recognize chilling as a low-temperature constraint on membranes, metabolism, photosynthesis, water transport and root function even when no frost occurs.
lessons.cultivation: Cold supply air, exterior surfaces, irrigation solution or power failures can create tissue conditions below the room average and can interact with condensation risk.
lessons.observe: Record minimum, duration, cooling and warming rate, leaf/root-zone temperature and delayed symptom development before diagnosing nutrient problems.

knowledgeChecks: Which processes can make a leaf warmer or cooler than the surrounding air?
Why is the laser dot on an IR thermometer not the full measurement area?
What evidence distinguishes warm conditions from heat stress?
Why can chilling injury occur without frost?

chapters.title: Humidity, Vapor Pressure, Dew Point & Condensation
chapters.objective: Interpret water vapor using temperature-aware quantities and identify condensation risk at plant and facility surfaces, especially during transitions.

lessons.title: Relative humidity changes when temperature changes
lessons.summary: Understand RH as the ratio of actual water vapor to the saturation capacity at that temperature rather than as an absolute amount of water in the air.
lessons.cultivation: The same moisture content can produce a different RH after air cools or warms, so RH trends must be interpreted alongside temperature.
lessons.observe: Use synchronized temperature and RH measurements from the same zone instead of combining values collected at different locations or times.

lessons.title: Saturation vapor pressure rises strongly with temperature
lessons.summary: Connect temperature to the maximum equilibrium vapor pressure of water, which underlies RH, dew point and VPD calculations.
lessons.cultivation: A temperature change modifies the vapor-pressure context even if no water vapor is added or removed.
lessons.observe: When comparing environmental periods, separate changes caused by moisture removal from changes caused primarily by temperature.

lessons.title: Dew point predicts when a surface can become wet
lessons.summary: Use dew point as the temperature at which the current vapor content reaches saturation and condensation can form on a sufficiently cool surface.
lessons.cultivation: Flowers, leaves, walls, ducts or containers can fall below dew point even while the room-average RH looks acceptable.
lessons.observe: Compare local surface or leaf temperature with dew point during lights-off, cold-air delivery and other rapid transitions.

lessons.title: Transitions can create short wet events hidden by averages
lessons.summary: Track lights-off cooling, equipment cycles, irrigation and thermal inertia because brief local condensation can disappear in hourly or room-average data.
lessons.cultivation: Dense reproductive tissue and cool surfaces can experience risk during a short transition even when the daily average climate seems stable.
lessons.observe: Use higher-frequency records around transitions and inspect high-risk surfaces rather than relying only on daily min/max summaries.

knowledgeChecks: Why can RH rise after lights turn off even if no new water vapor is added?
What is saturation vapor pressure and why does temperature matter?
What condition must occur for condensation to form on a surface?
Why can hourly averages miss biologically important wetness events?

chapters.title: VPD: Meaning, Calculation & Limits
chapters.objective: Use VPD as a physical descriptor of evaporative demand while avoiding universal setpoints, single-number diagnosis and confusion between air VPD and leaf VPD.

lessons.title: VPD is a vapor-pressure difference
lessons.summary: Define vapor pressure deficit as the difference between saturation vapor pressure and actual vapor pressure under a stated temperature basis.
lessons.cultivation: VPD summarizes atmospheric drying demand more directly than RH alone, but it does not reveal whether the roots can supply that demand.
lessons.observe: State the calculation method, temperature source and whether the value describes air or leaf conditions.

lessons.title: Air VPD and leaf VPD answer different questions
lessons.summary: Distinguish VPD calculated from air conditions from a leaf-centered calculation that uses measured leaf temperature and local vapor pressure.
lessons.cultivation: When leaf temperature differs materially from air temperature, a room-level air VPD can misrepresent the evaporative gradient at the tissue surface.
lessons.observe: Pair representative leaf temperature with synchronized local air measurements when using leaf VPD for diagnosis or study.

lessons.title: VPD influences transpiration but does not control it alone
lessons.summary: Connect VPD with stomatal conductance, boundary-layer conductance, radiation, root hydraulic supply and acclimation.
lessons.cultivation: Two plants at the same VPD can transpire differently because cultivar, stage, light, roots, leaf area and stomatal state differ.
lessons.observe: Interpret VPD with leaf temperature, substrate water status, water use and plant response rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.

lessons.title: A VPD chart is a starting hypothesis, not settled law
lessons.summary: Treat stage charts and target bands as provisional control envelopes that require facility, genotype and crop qualification rather than as universal recipes.
lessons.cultivation: Tight universal targets can cause excessive cycling or unsafe assumptions when sensors, equipment capacity, leaf temperature and crop state differ from the chart's context.
lessons.observe: Preserve the previous qualified recipe, define success and stop criteria, and review multiple plant and system measurements after a change.

knowledgeChecks: What physical difference does VPD describe?
When can air VPD differ substantially from leaf VPD?
Why can two plants at the same VPD transpire differently?
Why should a stage-based VPD chart be treated as a starting hypothesis?

chapters.title: Transpiration, Stomata & Root-Zone Supply
chapters.objective: Connect atmospheric demand to stomatal regulation, the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum and the root zone so wilting or high leaf temperature is not misread as an air-only problem.

lessons.title: Water moves through a soil-plant-atmosphere continuum
lessons.summary: Follow water from the root environment through plant tissues to the atmosphere along gradients in water potential and hydraulic resistance.
lessons.cultivation: Atmospheric demand matters only in relation to the plant's ability to acquire and transport water from its actual root zone.
lessons.observe: When plants lose turgor, assess substrate water status, salinity, roots, leaf temperature and demand together.

lessons.title: Transpiration links stomata, cooling and water transport
lessons.summary: Understand transpiration as water-vapor loss shaped by stomatal aperture, boundary layers, vapor-pressure gradient and water supply.
lessons.cultivation: A decline in transpiration can reduce leaf cooling while also signaling stomatal closure, low demand or root limitation.
lessons.observe: Compare water use, leaf temperature, substrate trend and visible posture before deciding whether transpiration is too high or too low.

lessons.title: A wet root zone can still fail to supply the shoot
lessons.summary: Separate water amount from water availability and root function by considering oxygen, salinity, temperature, disease, physical damage and sensor placement.
lessons.cultivation: Wilting in wet media does not prove the plant needs more irrigation and can worsen when root oxygen is already limited.
lessons.observe: Check root condition, drainage, substrate distribution and competing causes before adding water.

lessons.title: Drought and overwatering can converge on similar canopy symptoms
lessons.summary: Recognize that inadequate water supply and oxygen-limited roots can both reduce hydraulic delivery, stomatal function and growth while requiring very different corrective actions.
lessons.cultivation: Symptom appearance alone is weak evidence when opposite root-zone states can produce drooping, warm leaves or slowed growth.
lessons.observe: Use root-zone history and direct measurements to distinguish insufficient water from impaired uptake in a saturated zone.

knowledgeChecks: What does the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum describe?
How does transpiration contribute to leaf cooling?
Why can a plant wilt while the substrate is wet?
Which measurements help separate drought from hypoxia?

chapters.title: Air Movement, Ventilation & Moisture Removal
chapters.objective: Separate within-canopy mixing from air exchange and dehumidification while understanding boundary layers, distribution, equipment capacity and localized wind stress.

lessons.title: Leaf boundary layers resist heat, vapor and gas exchange
lessons.summary: Understand the slowed air immediately adjacent to plant surfaces and how leaf size, shelter, canopy density and air speed alter that resistance.
lessons.cultivation: Air movement can change leaf temperature, transpiration and CO2 exchange even without changing the room's total moisture content.
lessons.observe: Evaluate leaf and flower zones throughout the canopy rather than using visible motion at the top as proof of uniform mixing.

lessons.title: Circulation redistributes; it does not automatically remove moisture
lessons.summary: Distinguish mixing humid air within a space from exhausting that air, replacing it with drier air, or condensing water through dehumidification.
lessons.cultivation: Adding fans can reduce stagnant pockets while leaving the room's total water-vapor load nearly unchanged.
lessons.observe: Record fan state separately from HVAC, exhaust, intake and dehumidifier state when explaining humidity changes.

lessons.title: Uniform moderate distribution beats a damaging jet
lessons.summary: Treat airflow as a spatial distribution problem because a strong stream can desiccate or mechanically stress one zone while leaving another zone stagnant.
lessons.cultivation: Fan placement should be requalified as canopy height, density, trellis fill, filters and duct conditions change.
lessons.observe: Map multiple heights and inspect leaf temperature, edge curl, mechanical damage, drying pattern and condensation zones after adjustments.

lessons.title: Moisture-removal capacity must match crop load and transitions
lessons.summary: Connect plant evapotranspiration, irrigation, infiltration, lights-off cooling and equipment staging with the water that ventilation or dehumidification must actually remove.
lessons.cultivation: A system can hold acceptable average RH yet lose control during peak plant water release or rapid cooling if equipment capacity or control timing is insufficient.
lessons.observe: Track humidity rise rate, dew-point margin and equipment duty state across peak and transition periods.

knowledgeChecks: What is a leaf boundary layer and why does it matter?
Why can circulation improve mixing without lowering total room moisture?
How can stronger airflow create both a dry zone and a stagnant zone at the same time?
Which crop and operating events change the moisture-removal load?

chapters.title: CO2, Light, Ventilation & Safety Coordination
chapters.objective: Understand carbon dioxide as a measured photosynthetic input whose crop value depends on other resources and whose occupational safety controls must remain separate from plant optimization.

lessons.title: CO2 response depends on the rest of the photosynthetic system
lessons.summary: Connect elevated carbon dioxide response with light, temperature, water, mineral supply, healthy leaf area and sink capacity instead of treating CO2 as an independent yield dial.
lessons.cultivation: Adding CO2 cannot compensate for weak light, root dysfunction or another resource that has already become limiting.
lessons.observe: Document PPFD, temperature, leaf temperature, irrigation, nutrition, stage and actual canopy CO2 before attributing a crop response to enrichment.

lessons.title: Canopy demand and ventilation determine CO2 distribution
lessons.summary: Recognize that a dense lit canopy consumes CO2 while fans, injection points, leakage and ventilation shape the spatial concentration plants actually experience.
lessons.cultivation: A controller near an injection point can show target concentration while other crop zones are under-supplied or enrichment is being exhausted outdoors.
lessons.observe: Map canopy CO2 under actual lights and ventilation states rather than trusting one sensor.

lessons.title: Plant-control targets are not worker-safety limits
lessons.summary: Keep crop-control logic separate from independent occupational monitoring, alarms, ventilation, access controls and emergency procedures.
lessons.cultivation: A plant controller should not be treated as the life-safety system; compressed-gas or combustion installations require qualified design and current jurisdictional compliance.
lessons.observe: Verify independent safety sensors, alarm routing, shutdown and purge behavior rather than assuming the enrichment controller proves safe occupancy.

lessons.title: Evaluate enrichment with crop response, input mass and system losses
lessons.summary: Judge enrichment as a system intervention using measured plant response, CO2 consumption, ventilation losses, energy use, quality and equipment performance.
lessons.cultivation: Short-term leaf photosynthesis response does not guarantee proportional whole-crop yield, quality or economic return.
lessons.observe: Compare qualified enriched and baseline periods with enough context to identify whether another resource became limiting.

knowledgeChecks: Why does elevated CO2 not guarantee a proportional yield increase?
How can ventilation undermine enrichment efficiency?
Why must a crop CO2 controller remain separate from life-safety monitoring?
Which measurements are needed to evaluate whether enrichment is actually beneficial?

chapters.title: Control Envelopes, Transitions, Alarms & Records
chapters.objective: Turn environmental measurements into stage-aware control bands and auditable records without confusing setpoints, warnings, action limits or emergency conditions.

lessons.title: A setpoint is a controller request, not the plant condition
lessons.summary: Separate requested targets from measured room conditions, canopy distributions and tissue conditions while accounting for deadbands and equipment response.
lessons.cultivation: A controller can satisfy its local sensor while leaves, flowers or root zones remain outside the intended biological envelope.
lessons.observe: Compare target, controller sensor, mapped canopy conditions and plant measurements in the same time window.

lessons.title: Normal bands, warnings, actions and emergencies are different layers
lessons.summary: Design a hierarchy that distinguishes ordinary variation from conditions requiring attention, corrective action or safety/emergency response.
lessons.cultivation: Tight alarms without persistence rules or equipment capacity create cycling and alarm fatigue rather than better crop control.
lessons.observe: Document limit purpose, sensor/location, persistence time, response owner and recovery criteria for each alarm.

lessons.title: Transitions deserve their own environmental review
lessons.summary: Treat lights-on, lights-off, irrigation, door events, equipment staging and weather shifts as transient states that can produce risks hidden by steady-state averages.
lessons.cultivation: Rapid cooling can raise RH and reduce dew-point margin while plant transpiration, surface temperatures and dehumidification response are all changing at once.
lessons.observe: Use timestamped high-frequency data around transitions and compare equipment commands with actual measured response.

lessons.title: Environmental records should explain decisions, not just archive numbers
lessons.summary: Link sensor identity, raw data, equipment state, irrigation, crop stage, observations, alarms, interventions and outcomes into a traceable environmental record.
lessons.cultivation: A useful record lets later reviewers determine whether a crop change followed environment, irrigation, equipment failure, sensor error or management intervention.
lessons.observe: Preserve raw values, corrections, moved or replaced sensors and before/after maps whenever a control recipe changes.

knowledgeChecks: Why is a controller setpoint not the same thing as the plant environment?
How do warning, action and emergency limits differ?
Why should transitions be reviewed separately from steady-state averages?
Which records are required to reconstruct why an environmental decision was made?
